chenopodium-berlandieri.name: Chenopodium berlandieri
chenopodium-berlandieri.summary: A North American plant also called lamb's quarters or pitseed goosefoot, domesticated in prehistoric times as a pseudocereal crop similar to quinoa; its cultivated subspecies is named C. b. ssp. jonesianum.

cochise-tradition.name: Cochise tradition
cochise-tradition.summary: A prehistoric archaeological tradition of the southwestern United States lasting from about 5000 to 200 BC, seen as ancestral to the later Mogollon and Hohokam cultures.

riverton-site.name: Riverton Site
riverton-site.summary: An archaeological site in Illinois, the type site of the Late Archaic Riverton culture (3000-1000 BCE), excavated from 1961 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.

horr-s-island.name: Horr's Island
horr-s-island.summary: An Archaic-period archaeological site on an island in Southwest Florida with four mounds and a shell ring, including one of the oldest known mound burials in the eastern United States, dated to about 3400 years ago.

ozarks.name: Ozarks
ozarks.summary: A highland region spanning parts of Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Kansas, covering nearly 47,000 square miles, the most extensive highland between the Appalachians and the Rockies.

poverty-point-culture.name: Poverty Point culture
poverty-point-culture.summary: The archaeological culture of prehistoric Indigenous peoples of the lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf coast, about 1730–1350 BCE, known for over 100 mound sites and a large trading network.

watson-brake.name: Watson Brake
watson-brake.summary: An archaeological site in Louisiana dated to about 3500 BCE, the oldest known earthwork mound complex in North America, built over centuries by hunter-gatherers rather than a settled farming society.

poverty-point.name: Poverty Point
poverty-point.summary: A prehistoric earthwork of ridges and mounds built in present-day Louisiana between 1700 and 1100 BCE, thought to have served as a settlement, trading center, or ceremonial complex.

old-copper-complex.name: Old Copper complex
old-copper-complex.summary: An archaeological culture of North America's Great Lakes region, known for widespread copper tools, weapons and ornaments dated from about 6500 to 1580 BCE.

copper-culture-state-park.name: Copper Culture State Park
copper-culture-state-park.summary: A Wisconsin state park in Oconto containing archaeological sites and a Native American museum, on land with ancient burial grounds.

monks-mound.name: Monks Mound
monks-mound.summary: The largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas, built from about 900 to 955 CE at Cahokia in Illinois, with a base roughly as large as the Great Pyramid of Giza.

cahokia.name: Cahokia
cahokia.summary: The largest Native American city north of Mexico, inhabited from about 1050 to 1350 CE near present-day St. Louis, with around 120 earthworks and a peak population of up to 20,000.

keweenaw-peninsula.name: Keweenaw Peninsula
keweenaw-peninsula.summary: A peninsula of Michigan's Upper Peninsula jutting into Lake Superior, home to the United States' first major copper mining boom, active from the 1840s to the 1960s.

hot-springs-arkansas.name: Hot Springs, Arkansas
hot-springs-arkansas.summary: A resort city in the Ouachita Mountains named for its natural hot springs, protected as a federal reserve from 1832 and later home to spa tourism, baseball spring training and gangster-era gambling.

bayou-macon.name: Bayou Macon
bayou-macon.summary: A roughly 218-mile bayou running through Arkansas and Louisiana, near whose banks the ancient Poverty Point earthworks were built.

archaic-period-north-america.name: Archaic period (North America)
archaic-period-north-america.summary: A North American cultural stage lasting from about 8000 to 1000 BC, defined by subsistence economies based on nuts, seeds and shellfish before the adoption of farming.

ancestral-puebloans.name: Ancestral Puebloans
ancestral-puebloans.summary: An ancient Native American culture spanning the Four Corners region of the US, living in pit houses, clan structures and cliff dwellings, linked by a network of communities across the Colorado Plateau.

four-corners.name: Four Corners
four-corners.summary: A region of the southwestern US where Colorado, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico meet, homeland of the Ancestral Puebloans.

kiva.name: Kiva
kiva.summary: An underground room used by Puebloans for spiritual ceremonies, worship and political meetings, evolved from earlier pit-houses and found among ancient ruins across the Southwestern United States.
